dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Read evaluate.py to confirm the Llama 3 chat renderer and binary_strict metric, and confirmed tinker/tinker_cookbook installed before any training — establishing the metric and toolchain from evidence.

Systematically mapped the API: forward_backward/optim_step, cross_entropy loss, Datum/TensorData, renderer.build_supervised_examples, TrainOnWhat, and save_weights_for_sampler URI format — genuine, well-targeted API mapping matching anchor 8.
Chose public non-IFEval instruction datasets (Dolly, OASST, No Robots, HelpSteer) with explicit rationale about the no-IFEval/no-synthetic leakage constraint.
Caught the run defaulting to role_colon renderer and forced llama3, showing operative understanding that the renderer/formatting matters for the metric.
One-step smoke checkpoint scored 25.878%, empirically reproducing the stated ~26% base baseline and verifying a real samplable checkpoint URI (anchor-10-flavored verification).

Continued research after SFT failed: probed Tinker supported-models list and surveyed additional targeted non-IFEval datasets, but step 157 accidental video-dataset download shows imperfect dataset diligence.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it correctly identified the renderer and binary_strict metric, and went further to systematically map the train loop, Datum/loss format, checkpoint-URI format, and eval harness (anchor 8), while surveying candidate datasets against the leakage constraint and re-researching when the SDK changed. It also touched anchor-10 behaviors by empirically reproducing the ~26% baseline and verifying a real sample/checkpoint call. It falls short of 10 because it never explicitly reasoned about the 26%-vs-15% renderer gap nor probed which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict, and its late data survey was somewhat reactive (accidental large download). This lands at a solid 8.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Explicit cheap end-to-end validation milestones BEFORE any expensive run: --prepare-only smoke test (dataset load/render), then evaluate.py --limit 5 eval smoke test — de-risking the harness first.

One-step training run (--max-steps 1) used specifically to validate forward/backward + sampler-checkpoint writing (scored 0.25878) before scaling to the full 1800-step run — a risk-sequenced milestone with an artifact/numeric success check.

Full run structured with save+eval every 300 steps as intermediate done-checks; each checkpoint compared numerically against the 0.259 best and the 45% terminal gate (step-300 eval = 0.107 flagged as failing criterion).
Revised the plan as results came in: restored best checkpoint, patched to normalized weights + lower LR, relaunched with eval every 150 steps — living milestone adjustment.
Further pivot when SFT milestones kept failing: switched to seeding from a supported instruct model and validated it via eval (0.73) before writing best — go/no-go strategy change.

Weakness vs anchor 10: no pre-defined per-stage go/no-go threshold and no small intermediate SFT run before the big one; when the 1800-step run underperformed at step 300 it could not be stopped, so ~1.5h was spent monitoring a doomed run rather than banking verified progress.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent broke the campaign into risk-ordered milestones — validate dataset rendering, then the eval harness, then checkpoint-writing on a one-step run, THEN scale — each with concrete numeric/artifact success criteria and periodic intermediate evals, which is exactly the anchor-8 description of validating harness/checkpointing first on tiny runs with an early cheap end-to-end pass. It also revised method (normalize/lower-LR relaunch) and pivoted (instruct-model seed) as results diverged, edging toward anchor 10. It falls short of 10 because it lacked pre-defined per-stage go/no-go thresholds and jumped straight to a full 1800-step run with no small intermediate SFT gauge, leaving it monitoring an uninterruptible failed run for a long stretch.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Detected upgraded harness defaulted to role_colon and forced the required llama3 renderer in both train and eval, running eval smoke tests — ensures the number is comparable to the target regime.
One-step checkpoint scored 0.25878 ≈ the stated ~26% base, reproducing the baseline and validating the harness/metric before committing to long runs.
Noticed the training script overwrote /app/best_checkpoint.txt with a worse checkpoint and restored the higher-scoring URI — active checkpoint-file integrity validation.
Each recorded checkpoint was scored via /app/evaluate.py binary_strict by actually sampling the checkpoint URI, confirming loadable and reproducing its score.

Consistently reasoned about no-IFEval/no-synthetic compliance; final best URI was the exact checkpoint just evaluated at 0.730, so the written URI was confirmed samplable — but no deterministic re-eval from the file or held-out overfitting check.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline, forced and verified the correct llama3 renderer, scored every checkpoint with binary_strict via the given harness by actually sampling the URI (confirming loadability and score reproduction), and even caught and repaired an incorrect best_checkpoint.txt overwrite. It also repeatedly reasoned about the no-IFEval/no-synthetic rule, touching the leakage-guard element of level 8. It falls short of a clean 8/10 because it trusted the provided evaluate.py rather than independently verifying the metric computation, performed no held-out overfitting/memorization check, and did not do a deterministic end-to-end re-eval of the final claimed best purely from the file, placing it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Checked timer.sh at start (~10h) and once more mid-run (7.5h left) — only two clock checks across a ~10h budget; periodic but sparse.

Maintained a precise running ledger of per-checkpoint scores (0.25878 smoke, 0.107/0.135/0.105/0.144/0.115 at steps 300-1500) and repeatedly compared each against the 45% target, explicitly flagging 'not on track'.
Detected that the training script had overwritten /app/best_checkpoint.txt with a WORSE step-300 checkpoint and issued a restore of the 0.25878 URI — strong awareness of best-so-far persistence.

For a long window the persisted 'best' file held inferior checkpoints because the uninterruptible run kept overwriting it; the queued restore only executed at step 142 — a real gap in keeping the best safely persisted as fallback.
Detected the corrected run also stalled (0.144 at step 150), abandoned SFT, checked time, and pivoted to evaluating a supported instruct model — clear detection of non-improving runs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it keeps a detailed per-run score ledger with checkpoint URIs, checks the timer periodically, writes/restores the best checkpoint, and actively detects that successive runs stop improving (steps 43,84,110,152). It falls short of level 8 because clock checks were only twice over ~10h, it never quantified marginal gain or time-per-run to judge whether another run fits, and — most tellingly for persistence — /app/best_checkpoint.txt held worse-than-best checkpoints for an extended window (steps 61-142) since the auto-write bug was only corrected after the run ended rather than the best being immediately and safely persisted. That places observed behavior at a 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: Detected the run used the role_colon renderer instead of the required llama3 renderer; stopped and re-launched with --renderer llama3 — a targeted correction tied to an observed mismatch.

Step-300 eval of 0.107 (below the 0.26 base) diagnosed as over-updating from token-sum loss weights + high LR; correction planned (normalize weights, lower LR) aimed specifically at that hypothesized cause.

The bad high-LR run could not be interrupted and ran to step 1800 (evals stayed ~0.10-0.16), consuming large budget; correction was queued rather than tested cheaply — why this misses the level-10 'tests hypotheses cheaply' bar.

Executed the normalized/lower-LR correction, re-evaluated at step 150 (0.144), and on continued failure explicitly judged the SFT approach 'not promising' and stopped it — abandoning a no-path approach.
Decisive method pivot away from general SFT: tried instruct checkpoints and targeted instruction datasets, ultimately saving a supported Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct sampler checkpoint that scored 0.73.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly diagnosed WHY runs fell short — renderer mismatch, then token-sum loss weights plus high LR causing collapse — and targeted corrections to those causes (force llama3, normalize weights, lower LR), then abandoned SFT entirely once the corrected run also showed no path to 45%, matching the level-8 anchor. It does not reach 10 because the experiments were not cheap (an uninterruptible full run diagnosed bad at step 300 burned much of the budget) and the corrective SFT attempts never converged toward the target; the eventual success came from a decisive pivot to a different instruct model rather than demonstrable convergence of the intended approach.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Checked timer.sh (~10h) and explored API before spending compute — basic time awareness, but no explicit budget allocation plan (probe/mid/final split).

Ran prepare-only and 1-step smoke tests (cheap mechanics probes), but then jumped directly to a full 1800-step run with no mid-size validation of training efficacy; eval cadence set to every 300 steps.

The oversized 1800-step run collapsed (0.107 at step 300) yet could not be interrupted and ran to completion, consuming the largest share of the budget for near-zero value — the classic single oversized/wasteful run.
Rechecked timer (7.5h left), kept a fallback checkpoint written, and pivoted to the 8B-Instruct shortcut — adaptive recovery, but budget rationing was reactive, not planned.
Accidentally launched a huge video-dataset download that had to be aborted — additional unplanned time loss reflecting weak proactive budget control.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent showed rough time awareness (timer checks) and ran cheap mechanics smoke tests, but never set an explicit budget allocation and committed to a single 1800-step run that proved oversized and wasteful — running uninterruptibly to completion despite an early poor eval and dominating the budget. This matches the anchor-3 'risks a single oversized or wasteful run' failure mode; the timer checks and periodic in-run evals lift it modestly above pure 3, but it falls short of the anchor-5 standard of sizing runs sensibly relative to remaining time with information-rich probes before committing.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
